title: fix(css): order the nested list on what is written, not on what was
body:
**Summary**

The lowering writes the parent in front of each nested selector, and the list it splits was already canonical as the nested rule spelled it — so ordering it before the substitution settles nothing. `a{>b,+c,d{top:0}}` printed `a+c,a>b,a d` where a second pass writes `a d,a+c,a>b`: sorted on `>b,+c,d`, not on what the selectors became.

It is ordered after the substitution now, and only where there is a list to order — one selector is already the order it reads in, and asks nothing. Swiper 14 was the last shipped stylesheet carrying the shape and is clean.

Measured against a feature-off baseline in the same session, interleaved, best of nine: 6000 hoists writing a list of three cost 36.1 ms against 33.5 — the work is the ordering a second pass was doing anyway. Every other path is unchanged: 6000 hoists of one selector 25.7 ms against 25.7, 6000 hoists all distinct 25.7 against 25.4, 6000 flat rules 20.4 against 20.3. Output is byte-identical in all four, the order being a set's and not a length.

**What kind of change does this PR introduce?**

fix

**Did you add tests for your changes?**

Yes — three unit cases: a list of combinators ordered on the written selectors, a parent written as a list, and a selector the substitution turns into a twin being read back out, plus one holding a list the substitution leaves canonical. `configCases/css/minify-nested-combinator` gains the shape, read off the emitted stylesheet and checked against a second pass. Reverting the change fails one unit case and the config case, which I checked by doing it.

**Does this PR introduce a breaking change?**

No. A selector list is a set — the same selectors match the same elements in any order.

**If relevant, what needs to be documented once your changes are merged or what have you already documented?**

n/a

**Follow-up**

Five findings remain in the idempotence sweep under a target the lowerings run for, all in webpack's own fixtures — `css-modules`, `minimize-dead-rules`, `parsing/cases/nesting.css`, `parsing/cases/selectors.css` and `postcss-modules-local-by-default.pure`. They share one cause: where a hoist writes several rules, its text has no one prelude for the sheet to key it by, so neither the join nor the identical-rule drop can read it. `a{width:1px;.x{color:red}}.mid{color:teal}a{height:2px;.x{color:red}}` keeps both copies of `a .x{color:red}` where a second pass keeps one.

I wrote the narrow half of that — keying a hoist that wrote exactly one rule so the drop can take it back — and did not open it. It costs 11% on hoist-heavy sheets (6000 hoists all distinct, 28.5 ms against 25.6) for output that is byte-identical, and moves no finding in the corpus: the sweep reports the same five with it and without it. The shape it fixes has its own repro and is real, so it is worth doing where it earns something, not on its own.

**Use of AI**

AI was used. It reduced the sweep finding to `a{>b,+c,d{top:0}}`, wrote the change and the cases, measured the cost interleaved against a feature-off baseline, and broke the change to check a case catches it. The dedupe half was written, measured, and left out on the number. I reviewed the result.
